deck: Round 2: every base photo was reviewed by eye before re-annotating, and background chips were removed from all labels. Before/after pairs below show what changed and why.
description: A two-round QA pass on annotate_image. Round 1 placed labels from generic proportional guesses (analyze_image_layout does not detect faces or objects). Round 2 re-places every label using coordinates read directly off the actual photo, drops a fabricated product label and an inaccurate panorama caption, and removes background chips — with a measured legibility cost.

image.alt: Annotated mountain panorama with a title and caption overlay in amber

public.body: This article exists to exercise one thing on this platform: annotate_image's ability to place item names precisely relative to whatever is actually in a photo, in four different visual styles, in four different colors, across four very different kinds of images — a face, a panorama, a product shot, and a flat-lay of items on a table. Every label below was placed with normalized coordinates and a 6x6 layout grid, not eyeballed in an image editor.
public.title: Why This Test Exists

public.body: Before: arrows were placed from generic portrait proportions, without looking at the actual photo — Mouth and Chin both converged on the same mustache/upper-lip area, and Chin never reached the real chin. After: coordinates were read directly off the photo — Eyes now targets the man's actual right eye, Nose targets the nostril, Mouth drops to the true lip line, and Chin moves down and right to the visible skin above his fingers. Background chips were removed per instruction: with no backing, none of the four labels stayed OCR-legible (0/4), versus 1/4 (Mouth) when chips were present.

public.body: Before: the caption invented a scene that doesn't match the photo ("lake in evening light") and its background chips covered roughly 90% of this very short (2048×261) frame. After: the caption now describes what the photo actually shows — a bright, midday alpine valley with a village and green fields, no lake — and the chips are gone, so the photo itself is fully visible. Without a chip, neither the title nor the caption stayed OCR-legible on this image.

public.title: Panorama — Title & Caption Style, Amber (Before → After)

public.body: Before: the badges assumed a single bottle with a cap, pump, printed label, and body — but the photo actually shows four separate containers (a squeeze tube, a round jar, a foam-pump bottle, and a lotion pump bottle), and none of them carries a printed label, which is exactly what was flagged as missing. After: each of the four real containers is badged by name (Tube / Jar / Foam Pump / Lotion Bottle) and the fabricated "Label" callout is gone. The numbered badges are drawn shapes, not text, so they stayed legible either way; the legend caption text lost OCR legibility once its background chip was removed.

public.body: Before: arrows converged near the center of the frame regardless of what they were meant to label — "Notebook" pointed at the coffee cup, "Coffee Cup" pointed near the notebooks, and "Pen" missed the pen entirely. After: coordinates were read directly off the photo (Notebook, Coffee Cup, and Pen each targeted at their actual position), and all three arrows now land on the correct item. Legibility went the other way: 3/3 labels were OCR-legible with background chips, 0/3 without them.

public.title: Table Items — Label Style, Green (Before → After)

items: Round 1 (generic proportional guesses): internally consistent but not anchored to the real subject — face labels landed about one grid row too high, the table's three labels were effectively swapped between items, and the product badges assumed a single-bottle anatomy the photo doesn't have.

Round 2 (coordinates read directly from the source photos): every arrow now lands on its correct item, confirmed by eye against the actual base image rather than the layout grid. The renderer places exactly what it's told, precisely — round 1's misses were entirely a coordinate-input problem, not a rendering problem.
Products were relabeled to match what's actually in the photo (Tube / Jar / Foam Pump / Lotion Bottle) instead of a fabricated "Label" callout on a bottle that has no printed label.
The panorama's caption was corrected from an invented "lake in evening light" to what the photo actually shows: a sunlit valley, no lake, no evening light.

Background chips were removed from every label in round 2 as requested. The effect on legibility was severe: OCR matched 8 of 13 label/title/caption strings across the two chipped rounds, versus 0 of 13 with no chip — the chips were not just cosmetic, they were carrying most of the real-world legibility.

Open from round 1, unchanged: the contrast checker's reported ratio did not move when a background chip was resized larger, suggesting it samples the composite more narrowly than the chip's actual footprint — worth a look on the pdf-tool side.
create_agent_artifact_job (AI image generation) is still out of credits; round 2 reused the same Wikimedia Commons source photos as round 1.
